newsitem.title: USA: Indonesia denies Timor human rights charges.
newsitem.headline: Indonesia denies Timor human rights charges.

text.p: The Indonesian Embassy in Washington on Tuesday called charges by a U.S. congressman of human rights violations in East Timor biased and inaccurate.

The charges of widespread killings, torture and other violations by Indonesian military and police came in a news conference last Thursday by Representative Frank Wolf, a Virginia Republican, who visited East Timor the previous week.
"The picture Mr. Wolf paints of East Timor is so blatantly inaccurate that we feel compelled to respond," the embassy said in a statement.

"We feel Congresman Wolf's detailed reflections of his brief tour are biased, one-sided and represent a perspective doubtless cemented prior to his visit and completely unaffected by the reality of life today on East Timor," the embassy said in a statement.
Wolf said he based his findings on interviews with residents of East Timor. He also met Indonesian officials in Jakarta.

"We have been more sensitive to the rights of the people of East Timor and have done more to enhance the quality of life of East Timor's people in 20 short years than over 450 years of Portuguese colonial servitude," the embassy said.

Indonesia took over the former Portuguese colony in December, 1975 and incorporated it as a province the following July. The United Nations did not recognise the move and still regards Portugal as the territory's administering power.

In Jakarta, Indonesian Foreign Minister Ali Alatas said on Tuesday he and United Nations Secretary General Kofi Annan would discuss the future of U.N.-sponsored talks with Portugal on East Timor in Switzerland next week.
Alatas will attend the World Economic Forum meeting in Davos, Switzerland from Jan. 30 to Feb. 4.
"I expect to meet the secretary-general at the Davos meeting... I will ask about future talks on East Timor with Portugal," Alatas said.
